en: Homage to the Buddha.

Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain, in the palace called the Womb of the Dharmadhātu, which has peaks of infinite jewels, together with a great community of monks, twenty-five thousand in number;
all of whom were arhats, whose taints were exhausted, who were free from afflictions, who had attained mastery, and whose minds and wisdom were well-liberated.

[He was accompanied] by well-bred great elephants who had accomplished their task, finished what was to be done, laid down their burdens, achieved their own goal, exhausted the fetters of existence, whose minds were perfectly liberated through right knowledge, and who had attained the supreme perfection of mastery over all mental states;
and by sixty-eight great śrāvakas, headed by Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya.
Together with seventy-two hundred thousand nayutas of kotis of bodhisattvas,
such as the youthful Mañjuśrī,
the bodhisattva mahāsattvas Dhanaśrī, Buddhiśrī, Bhaiṣajyarāja, and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata.
All were turners of the irreversible wheel of Dharma; all were skilled in inquiring about the extensive Ratnakūṭa Sūtra; and all had attained the stage of the Cloud of Dharma.
They were like Mount Sumeru in their wisdom;
all of them were thoroughly permeated by the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-birth, and non-existence;
they were radiant with the manifestation of the most profound Dharma.
They possessed the majestic deportment of Tathāgatas, were sent from hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Tathāgatas in various world-systems,
were all produced through the cultivation of the superknowledges, and were established in the intrinsic nature of the reality of all phenomena.
Then, at that time, this thought occurred to the Blessed One:
"What if I were to deliver a Dharma discourse for the sake of generating great speed, power, momentum, and strength in the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas;
and what if I were to assemble the most majestic Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, from as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges?"
Suppose now that I were to manifest a sign for the purpose of illuminating this great exposition of the Dharma, and produce a great radiance,
so that the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, might come and inquire about this great exposition of the Dharma.

Then, at that time, the Blessed One illuminated world-systems in the ten directions— world-systems equal in number to the atoms within incalculable, inconceivable trichiliocosm great world-systems— with clouds of great rays of light.

Furthermore, at that moment, from each of the ten directions, there arrived bodhisattvas equal in number to the atoms within hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of inexpressible Buddha-fields.
The great beings arrived;

each one of those bodhisattva mahāsattvas, having come by means of inconceivable bodhisattva transformations, performed an inconceivable worship befitting the Blessed One, [seated] upon thrones produced by the power of their respective vows.
They sat down on lotus seats in front of the Blessed One and remained there,
gazing at the Blessed One with unblinking eyes.
Then, at that time, in the center of the palace within the Dharmadhātugarbha, a lion throne appeared, having the essence of a great jewel lotus;
it was many tens of millions of *yojanas* in extent and rose up in regular gradation.
It was composed entirely of all-illuminating precious gems, possessed lamps of lightning,
and was surrounded by a railing of precious jewels.
It had a handle made of a jewel-gem of inconceivable radiance, was surrounded by a retinue of incomparable jewel-gems,
and was adorned with a garland of jewel-gems whose power surpassed that of the incomparable.
It was covered by a net of *vaśirāja* jewel-kings,
inlaid with various precious gems, and adorned with raised parasols, banners, and flags.
And from above that great lion throne, which had a lotus-heart made of precious jewels, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of incalculable rays of light issued forth in all directions.
Those rays pervaded the world-systems in the ten directions with a great radiance, one after another.
Furthermore, at that time, from each of the ten directions, there came [Bodhisattvas] as numerous as the atoms in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of unspeakable Buddha-fields.
Gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the world-protectors arrived there.
Among them, some arrived seated within precious gabled palaces, accompanied by the sounds of music played by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of innumerable and inconceivable apsarases.
Some were made of flowers,
some of uragasāra sandalwood,
and some of pearls.
Some were made of diamond,
some were made of vajra-luminous maṇi jewels,
and some were made of Jāmbūnada gold.
Some were made of the king of jewels that gathers all radiance;
some were made of the vaśirāja jewel;
and some were made of the wish-fulfilling jewel.

Some arrived mounted upon wheels made of jewels, while others came seated within gabled palaces made of great precious jewels— such as the *sāgarapratiṣṭhāna-viśuddha-ratna-vyūha-samantaraśmi-prabhā-maṇi*— which resounded with the music performed by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of incalculable and inconceivable celestial nymphs.
Having arrived, they performed an inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, and boundless worship of the Blessed One,
and sat down to one side upon seats produced by their own past vows.
Having sat down, they remained gazing at the Blessed One with unblinking eyes.
Furthermore, at that time, this triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system became composed of Jāmbūnada gold;
it was adorned with various great maṇi-jewel trees, divine flower trees, clothing trees, and fragrant uragasāra sandalwood trees,
and was completely covered by a net of moon, sun, lightning, lamps, and maṇi-jewels.
With parasols, banners, and flags raised high,
all the trees stood there, attended by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of incalculable apsarases who held strings of pearl necklaces and great garlands of precious jewels.
Then, at that time, from that lion-throne within the great jewel-lotus heart, these verses issued forth:
"Come and sit down, O King of Men! For I have arisen through the power of your merit.
My resolve is fulfilled; today I shall support you, the Jina, the supreme among bipeds."
Indeed, this body of mine is composed of jewels, and a single jewel-lotus stands in my midst;
it is beautiful for your sake, O Leaders. O Protectors, fulfill my aspiration this very day!
Sitting upon this lotus made of jewels, please grace me and this entire world;
teach the Dharma to many millions of living beings, so that they may obtain such a lion-throne as this upon hearing it.
The thousands of rays produced from your body illuminate many world-systems;
this is indeed the mark of one who has attained joy. O Leaders, please step forward for my sake.
Please sit down quickly and grant us your favor; O Blessed One, in this place where eight crores of self-arisen sages were previously supported by me, please show your grace today.

Then the Blessed One, having risen from his previous seat and sat down upon that lion-throne in the center of a great jewel-lotus, assumed the cross-legged posture and gazed upon the entire assembly of bodhisattvas;
he then gave a sign to those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas for the purpose of an exalted teaching of the Dharma.
Then, at that time, the entire assembly of bodhisattvas thought to themselves:
"If only this Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta would question the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding non-arising and non-cessation; for we have not heard this Dharma-discourse for a long time."
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having perceived a sign from the Blessed One and having understood with his own mind the reflection in the minds of those bodhisattva mahāsattvas,
addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, it is said that there is 'non-arising' and 'non-ceasing'."
"Blessed One, of what dharma is this the designation: 'non-arising' and 'non-ceasing'?
And he spoke these verses:
'O Guide, you speak of non-ceasing and non-arising.'"
O one of great wisdom, what is the definition and etymology of that?
How is this "neither ceasing nor arising" described?
O Great Sage, please explain it through both analogies and logical reasons.
These many bodhisattvas seeking wisdom have come together, O Lord, to pay homage to you; they have been sent by the guides of the world. Please teach the sublime and supreme True Dharma.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī! It is indeed excellent, Mañjuśrī, that you consider it necessary to ask the Tathāgata about this matter."

Mañjuśrī, you have set out for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of the great mass of beings— both gods and humans— and for the purpose of enabling the bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have arrived here to attain the stage of a Buddha.
"Mañjuśrī, you should apply yourself to this point without fear; there is no need for terror or paralysis.
And, Mañjuśrī, you must rely upon wisdom."
As the Tathāgata explains this meaning:
Mañjuśrī, "non-arising" and "non-ceasing" are designations for the Tathāgata.
For example, Mañjuśrī, suppose this great earth were established as being composed of great beryl.

And it should be so arranged that the reflection of the abode of the Thirty-three, of Śakra, the lord of the gods, and of the Vaijayanta palace might be clearly seen upon that great earth made of beryl.
And Śakra, the lord of the gods, would be seen there sporting, enjoying himself, and being entertained by the five divine qualities of sensual pleasure.
Then, at that time, the gods would exhort all the men, women, boys, and girls of Jambudvīpa:
"Come, O men and women!"
"Behold this Śakra, the lord of the gods, in the Vaijayanta palace, playing, sporting, and enjoying himself with the five divine qualities of sensual pleasure! Come, O throngs of men and women!
Give gifts and perform meritorious deeds!"
And by undertaking and abiding in moral discipline,
you will play, rejoice, and enjoy yourselves in such Vaijayanta palaces, and you will exercise the sovereignty of Śakra; moreover,
you will be endowed with such supernatural power.
And just as Śakra, the lord of the gods, was endowed and possessed of divine enjoyments,
so too, Mañjuśrī, those men, women, boys, and girls [beheld] upon that great earth made of beryl the abode of the Thirty-three, the Vaijayanta palace, and...
Having seen the manifestation of Śakra, the lord of the gods, they would join their palms in reverence,
scatter flowers, scatter perfumes, and speak these words:
"May we also become such as Śakra, the lord of the gods; may we also sport, rejoice, and dwell in the Vaijayanta palace just as this Śakra, the lord of the gods does.
Yet those beings did not perceive it in this way.

This is a reflection appearing on the great earth made of beryl, wherein the abode of the Thirty-three, the Vaijayanta palace, and Śakra, the lord of the gods, are all seen as reflections because of the utter purity of the great beryl.
Delighting in the state of Śakra, they give gifts,
perform meritorious deeds,
and abide having undertaken the precepts of moral conduct.
And there, in the abode of the Thirty-three, they dedicate their roots of merit for the sake of rebirth;
yet, Mañjuśrī, although that great earth is made of lapis lazuli, there is no abode of the Thirty-three there,
nor is there the Vaijayanta palace.
Nor is Śakra, the lord of the gods,
visible; rather, because of the purity of the great lapis lazuli, the abode of the Thirty-three and the Vaijayanta palace are clearly seen.
Śakra is the lord of the gods;
yet he neither arises nor ceases, for due to the purity of the great lapis lazuli, his reflection is seen.
In the same way, Mañjuśrī, because of the purity of the mind and the thorough cultivation of meditation, the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s own body appears to sentient beings.
By the power of the Tathāgata, Mañjuśrī, sentient beings perceive the Tathāgata;

yet he is unreal, unarisen, and unceasing; neither an entity nor a non-entity, neither visible nor invisible, neither worldly nor unworldly, neither a shrine nor a non-shrine, neither existent nor non-existent.
Nevertheless, Mañjuśrī, sentient beings take this manifestation of the Tathāgata as their objective support and scatter flowers.
They scatter perfumes, garments, and jewels,
and speak these words:
"May we also become such as the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Desiring the wisdom of a Buddha, they give gifts,
perform meritorious deeds,
and abide having undertaken ethical discipline.
And they dedicate that root of merit toward the attainment of the Tathāgata’s knowledge.
Mañjuśrī, it is just as, for example, the reflection of Śakra, the lord of the gods, does not stir upon that great earth made of great vaidūrya.
He does not conceive,
he does not proliferate, and he does not conceptualize.
He does not conceptualize.

He is without thought, without conceptualization, inconceivable, without mental engagement, peaceful, cooled, unarisen, unceasing, unseen, unheard, unsmelled, untasted, untouched, signless, non-cognitive, and incapable of being made known.
In this very way, Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha, does not move.
He does not conceive,
he does not proliferate, and he does not conceptualize.
He does not conceptualize.

He is without thought, without conceptualization, inconceivable, beyond mental engagement, peaceful, cooled, unarisen, unceasing, unseen, unheard, unsmelled, untasted, untouched, signless, non-communicative, and incapable of being made known.
For, Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata has the nature of non-arising.
And yet, like a reflection, he appears in the worlds;
and according to the diverse inclinations of sentient beings, he displays a diversity in the measure of his lifespan through the diversity of his manifestations.
By means of bringing beings to maturity and establishing them in the power of resolute conviction, he becomes manifest to those beings who are vessels for awakening;
and according to their inclinations and convictions, beings hear the Dharma,
perceiving it as the three vehicles in accordance with their own dispositions.
And they resolve according to their respective inclinations.

It is just as, Mañjuśrī, for the gods of the Trayastriṃśa heaven, who have been perfected through the power of their merit, there is the great Dharma drum that produces sounds of the Dharma; it is situated in the sky above the Vaijayanta palace, invisible to all the sons of the gods.
And yet, Mañjuśrī, that great Dharma drum—

At whatever time the gods belonging to the Trāyastriṃśa host become intoxicated by intense, constant, and continuous divine pleasures, amusements, delights, and enjoyments, they no longer enter the Sudharmā assembly hall of the gods to chant the Dharma together;
and when Śakra, the lord of the gods, becomes intoxicated by divine pleasures, amusements, delights, and enjoyments, [the same occurs].

He does not sit upon the Dharma-seat to preach the Dharma. At that time, Mañjuśrī, that great Dharma-drum— invisible, imperceptible, having transcended the range of sight, and situated in the sky— emits such a sound of Dharma by which it makes itself known through its voice to all the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa realm.
"Friends, form, sound, smell, taste, and touch are impermanent; do not live in negligence, lest you quickly fall away from this state of existence.
Friends, all conditioned phenomena are suffering."
"Friends, all conditioned phenomena are without self;
friends, all conditioned phenomena are empty. Do not fall into negligence!
For those who pass away from here, there will be rebirth again in this very place, which is suffering."
Sing together, friends, the Dharma;
be those who delight in the pleasure grove of the Dharma, whose essence is the Dharma,
and who incline toward the Dharma.
"Inclined toward the Dharma and attending to the recollection of the Dharma,
O friends, dwell once more with these very divine pleasures, sports, delights, and enjoyments."
"You shall not be separated from it.

At that time, Mañjuśrī, there arose the great Dharma drum— unseen, formless, inconceivable, non-conceptual, transcending the path of sight, unarisen and unceasing, transcending the path of speech, and free from mind, intellect, and consciousness.
By that sound, all the gods belonging to the realm of the Thirty-three were exhorted; terrified, trembling, and deeply agitated,
they entered the Sudharmā assembly hall of the gods and dwelt there, delighting in the pleasure of the garden of Dharma,
having the Dharma as their essence.
They become inclined toward the Dharma, leaning toward the Dharma,
and possess mental attention directed toward the recollection of the Dharma.
Having passed away from there, they become those who attain excellence.
At that time, Śakra, the lord of the gods, enters the Sudharmā assembly hall of the gods, sits upon the Dharma-throne, and teaches the Dharma.
And when, Mañjuśrī, the asuras engage in battle with the gods, [they attain excellence].
In that regard, when the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three suffer defeat,
then that Dharma-drum emits such a sound that,
by that sound, the asuras— terrified, trembling, and utterly agitated— flee.
Moreover, Mañjuśrī, that great dharma drum has no producer, nor does it possess any physical form.
Mañjuśrī, that great dharma drum is invisible, imperceptible, non-existent, unreal, mindless, insentient, signless, formless, soundless, bodiless, non-dual, and beyond the range of the eye.
Nevertheless, Mañjuśrī, the sound of the great dharma drum issues forth for those sons of the gods belonging to the Trayastriṃśa heaven who have performed their prior preparations.
It serves to pacify all calamities, distresses, and afflictions of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.

Mañjuśrī, just as that great drum is invisible, without a self-substance, imperceptible, non-existent, unreal, inconceivable, insentient, signless, formless, soundless, non-being, non-dual, and beyond the range of the eye;

Through the ripening of his past karma, a sound issues forth for the sake of pacifying all calamities, distresses, and secondary afflictions of the sons of the gods belonging to the realm of the Thirty-three.
It also urges on with the sound of the Dharma those sons of the gods who are heedless.
And that sound of the Dharma conduces to the pacification of all calamities, distresses, and secondary afflictions of the sons of the gods belonging to the realm of the Thirty-three.

In the same way, Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is invisible, unobservable, without personal existence, non-existent, unoriginated, mindless, insentient, signless, formless, soundless, non-dual, and without being;
he has transcended the path of the eye.
Nevertheless, Mañjuśrī, through the ripening of their former karma and according to their inclinations and resolute beliefs, sentient beings perceive the sound of the Dharma issuing forth.
And that sound of the Dharma conduces to the pacification of all calamities, distresses, and secondary afflictions for all sentient beings.
By means of the resonance of the voice of the Dharma, it is reckoned in the world as the "voice of the Tathāgata.
Yet, Mañjuśrī, there is no such thing as a Tathāgata.
Nevertheless, through the resonance of the voice of Dharma, the designation "Tathāgata" arises in the world.
It is solely by virtue of the ripening of the former wholesome karma of sentient beings that beings perceive the word "Tathāgata" issuing forth.
This sound issues forth for the sake of generating all happiness for all sentient beings and for the purpose of exhorting those who are heedless.
Mañjuśrī, when those beings hear that sound, they conceive the thought of the Tathāgata,
[thinking], "This is the physical body of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, the voice of the Tathāgata is heard for the sake of generating roots of merit directed toward the Tathāgata among beginner bodhisattvas and all ordinary worldlings.
Moreover, Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata should be understood as neither arisen nor ceased.
Mañjuśrī, it is just as follows: at the end of the summer heat, when the first month of the rainy season has arrived, by the ripening of the former karma of sentient beings,

such winds blow in the sky above, in the intermediate space, for the purpose of generating all grasses, shrubs, medicinal herbs, and forest trees, as well as the multitude of seeds and the multitude of living beings situated upon the earth.
From that, water arises;
once arisen, it falls upon the great earth,
and by that, the entire great earth is thoroughly saturated.
At that time, all the beings of Jambudvīpa become joyful;
having given rise to gladness, the designation "cloud" arises in the world for him.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, at whatever time a great mass of water does not fall from the sky above,
at that time all the beings of Jambudvīpa think:
"No cloud exists here."
But when, Mañjuśrī, a great mass of water falls from the sky above onto the great earth,
sentient beings say:
"Oh, the great cloud releases water and satiates the great earth!"
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, neither cloud nor the designation "cloud" exists here.
Mañjuśrī, a great mass of water produced by the wind falls from the sky above;
that mass of water, Mañjuśrī, vanishes right there in the sky.
Due to the ripening of the previous karma of sentient beings,

Mañjuśrī, just as that mass of water in the intermediate space, being obstructed by the agitation of the wind while discharging water, receives the designation "cloud," so too it is due to the ripening of the previous karma of sentient beings.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, no cloud exists here, nor is there any designation of a cloud.
Mañjuśrī, the cloud is unarisen and unceasing; it does not enter the course of the mind and is liberated from coming and going.
In the same way, Mañjuśrī, for those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have accumulated the equipment of roots of merit from the past,

for other beings whose intention is directed toward the knowledge of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and for those beings who have planted roots of merit and for whom the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has become the cause for demonstrating the path to nirvāṇa, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses unhindered eloquence.
He comes to be reckoned as one "born in the world.
Whatever he speaks is all such, not false, and not otherwise;
therefore, among gods and humans, the name "Tathāgata" is given to him.
And yet, Mañjuśrī, the sound "Tathāgata" issues forth among gods and humans;
however, Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata does not exist.
Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata is signless, free from signs, neither staying in a place nor staying outside a place.
It is unreal, unarisen, and unceasing. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, that reflection of the Tathāgata, having satisfied and gladdened the world with its gods through the Dharma,
becomes invisible due to the ripening of past karma for beginner bodhisattvas, others, and all foolish ordinary persons who are to be disciplined by means of nirvāṇa.
It occurs to them that "the Tathāgata has entered final nirvāṇa.
But, Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata neither arises nor ceases.
Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata is unarisen and unceasing;
Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is primordially parinirvṛta.
Just as it is, Mañjuśrī...

Just as, with water as a basis, there exists in the world the designation "cloud" for a cloud that is unreal, unarisen, unceased, and non-existent; even so, Mañjuśrī, with the teaching of the Dharma as a basis, there exists in the world the designation by name "Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha" for a Tathāgata who is unreal, unarisen, unceased, and non-existent from the very beginning, being unborn from the outset.
Mañjuśrī, it is just as if the Great Brahmā Anabhibhū, who exercises mastery over ten trichiliocosms, were to survey all the assemblies of devas day after day,

down to the assembly of the Cāturmahārājika devas. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, at that time, while that Great Brahmā, the master of ten trichiliocosms, was surveying all the assemblies of devas, [he saw...]

In all the assemblies of the gods, all the sons of the gods— having abandoned their respective sports, pleasures, and enjoyments of desire, and having silenced the music of all the cymbals and instruments— having cast aside their mental preoccupation with the pleasures of desire, looked upon Mahābrahmā with reverence and unblinking eyes, joining their palms in homage.
And that Mahābrahmā granted his presence for a moment to all the assemblies of the gods.
And at that time, those sons of the gods desired rebirth in the realm of Mahābrahmā,

and they dedicated their roots of merit for the sake of rebirth in the realm of Mahābrahmā. And Mañjuśrī, that Great Brahmā, while not falling from that Brahma-palace, presided over another Great Brahmā.

By the power of his former vows and through the accumulation of the roots of virtue by those sons of the gods, Mañjuśrī manifested as a Great Brahmā who exercises mastery over ten trichiliocosms; and that manifested Great Brahmā surveys all the assemblies of gods day after day.
As far as the realm of the gods belonging to the Four Great Kings,

at that time, Mañjuśrī, all the sons of the gods in every divine assembly abandoned their respective amusements, sports, pleasures, and enjoyments; having relinquished their mental attentions toward amusements, sports, and pleasures, they paid reverent homage with palms joined and gazed unwinkingly at Mahābrahmā.
And that Mahābrahmā grants his vision to all the classes of gods for a moment,
yet he does not move from his place;
and at that time, those sons of the gods desire rebirth in the world of Mahābrahmā.
And they dedicate their roots of merit for rebirth in the Brahma-world.
Yet, Mañjuśrī, no Brahmā exists here.

Mañjuśrī, this Brahmā is empty; he is insubstantial, unreal, without letters, without sound, without location, non-existent, inconceivable, signless, free from mind, thought, and consciousness, unarisen, and unceasing.

Moreover, Mañjuśrī, Mañjuśrī appears as a vision within all the assemblies of gods through the empowerment of the former roots of merit and vows of that very Mahābrahmā, and through the accumulation of the former roots of merit of those sons of gods;
yet, Mañjuśrī, it does not occur to those sons of gods:
"This Brahmā is an emanation;
he is empty, insubstantial, unreal, without syllables, without sound, without location, non-existent, inconceivable, signless, free from mind, thought, and consciousness, unarisen, and unceasing.

In the very same way, Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is also empty, insubstantial, unreal, without syllables, without sound, without location, non-existent, inconceivable, signless, and free from mind, thought, and consciousness.
"Unarisen and unceasing; yet, Mañjuśrī, through the empowerment of his former vows and the practice of a bodhisattva, the Tathāgata, Arhat,
Samyaksaṃbuddha [appears] to beginner bodhisattvas, to all those who have set out in the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and to all foolish ordinary beings."

Through the empowerment of all roots of goodness, the Tathāgata— adorned with hundreds of thousands of marks— is seen in the world like a reflection, yet he does not move from his place. And, Mañjuśrī, it does not occur to beginner bodhisattvas, nor to those belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, nor to any foolish ordinary people, that [he has moved].

"The Tathāgata is empty, insubstantial, unreal, without syllables, without sound, without location, non-existent, inconceivable, signless, free from mind, intellect, and consciousness, unarisen, and unceasing. And yet, Mañjuśrī, from the body of the Tathāgata— adorned with hundreds of thousands of marks— there issues forth a great teaching of the Dharma for the sake of various and diverse beings of manifold inclinations, even within the emptiness of all the Tathāgatas' modes of conduct."
And that teaching of the Dharma leads to the pacification of all calamities, distresses, and secondary afflictions for all sentient beings.
In this regard, the Tathāgata is equanimous toward all, free from conceptual construction, and without distinction.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī, by this method as well, it should be understood in this way.
"Non-arising and non-cessation" is a designation for the Tathāgata.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"The Tathāgata is eternally of the nature of non-arising, and all phenomena are identical to the Sugata.
Yet, through the grasping of signs, those of childish intellect wander among unreal phenomena in the world."
For the Tathāgata is a reflection of wholesome, untainted phenomena;
yet herein there is neither suchness nor a Tathāgata, and yet an image appears throughout the entire world.
It is just as, Mañjuśrī, when the rays of the sun first illuminate the great king of mountains, Sumeru, in Jambūdvīpa;
thereafter they illuminate the Cakravāḍas and the Mahācakravāḍas;
and thereafter they illuminate the increasingly higher regions of the earth.
Thereafter, Mañjuśrī, those rays of the sun illuminate the low-lying regions of the earth here in Jambūdvīpa; yet those rays of the sun do not conceptualize,
nor do they discriminate.
They do not think, nor do they reflect;
Mañjuśrī, the rays of the sun are devoid of mind, intellect, and consciousness.
Unarisen and unceasing, without characteristics and free from characteristics, without mental engagement and free from mental engagement.
They are without conceptual proliferation, free from conceptual proliferation;
they are without feverish distress, free from feverish distress;
they do not stand on this shore, nor do they stand on the other shore.
Neither high nor low,
neither bound nor liberated,
neither possessors of knowledge nor devoid of knowledge.
They are neither afflicted nor free from affliction;
they are neither speakers of truth nor speakers of falsehood;
they are neither on the shore nor in the depths.
It is neither on dry land nor in water;
it is neither within the sphere of logic nor outside the sphere of logic.
Nevertheless, Mañjuśrī, according to the distinctions of high, low, and middle upon the earth, there occurs a variety of shadows corresponding to inferior, middling, and superior illumination.
In the very same way, Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, does not conceptualize, does not discriminate,
and does not think.
He does not engage in discursive thought;
Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata is free from mind, intellect, and consciousness, unarisen and unceasing.
It is without characteristics, free from characteristics; it is without mental attention, free from mental attention;
it is without conceptual proliferation, free from conceptual proliferation.
Free from burning, without fever;
standing neither on this shore nor on the further shore,
neither high nor low.
Neither bound nor liberated,
neither possessing knowledge nor lacking knowledge,
neither afflicted nor free from affliction.
Neither a speaker of truth nor a speaker of falsehood,
neither in the low nor in the high,
neither on dry land nor in water.
Neither with a current nor without a current, neither omniscient nor non-omniscient,
neither reasoning nor non-reasoning, and without movement.
Neither non-activity,
nor engagement, nor non-engagement;
neither possessing mindfulness, nor lacking mindfulness.
Neither conscious nor unconscious,
neither mind nor non-mind,
neither born nor unborn.
It is neither designatable nor non-designatable; it is neither a guide nor a non-guide;
it is neither a leader on the path nor a leader away from the path.

Neither one who has attained the fruit nor one who has not attained the fruit; neither conceptual construction nor non-conceptual construction; neither one who has transcended conceptual construction nor one who has not transcended conceptual construction.
Moreover, Mañjuśrī, the rays of wisdom from the sun-disk of the Tathāgata emit an unimpeded radiance throughout the triple world and the infinite, centerless realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Once these rays have been emitted, they first fall upon the bodies of those bodhisattvas whose resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) is like that of the great king of mountains;
only after that do they fall upon the bodies of those who have set out in the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas.
After that, they fall upon the bodies of those who have set out in the vehicle of the śrāvakas;
after that, they fall upon the bodies of beings with virtuous resolute intentions according to their respective inclinations;
and finally, the rays from the solar disc of the Tathāgata fall even upon the bodies of those beings whose mental continuums are fixed in falsehood.
And they become benefactors to them by generating the causes for the future and by causing them to flourish through wholesome qualities.
In that regard, Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata is equal toward all, impartial, free from conceptual construction, and without distinction.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, it does not occur to the sun-disk of the Tathāgata’s wisdom:
"I shall teach the sublime Dharma to this being."
He does not form such a conceptual discrimination as, "I shall not teach this to him," nor does he think,
"This being is one whose resolve is sublime."
This one has middling resolve; this one has resolve for the Śrāvaka vehicle;
this one has a virtuous intention.
"‘This one has an inferior and false intention’—Mañjuśrī, such a thought does not occur to the sun-disk of the Tathāgata’s wisdom:
‘This being possesses a noble intention and inclination; I shall teach the Mahāyāna to him.’"
"This one has an inclination toward the middling resolve; I shall teach him the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.
This one is inclined toward the Śrāvaka vehicle; I shall teach him the Śrāvaka vehicle.
And having understood the inclinations of sentient beings whose intentions are both wholesome and unwholesome, I shall purify them."
I shall cultivate a straight view;
I shall teach the Dharma according to what is appropriate even for those beings fixed in falsehood.
Such conceptualization does not occur to the radiance of the rays from the solar disk of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
For what reason?
Because the radiance of the rays from the solar disc of the Tathāgata’s wisdom has completely severed all conceptual constructions, discriminations, and proliferations.

Nevertheless, Mañjuśrī, due to the diversity in the continuums of the virtuous intentions of sentient beings, there occurs a diversity in the radiance of the rays from the solar disc of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
For example, Mañjuśrī, in the great ocean there is a great jewel called "Fulfiller of All Intentions," which is fastened to the top of a banner.
Whatever kind of intention a sentient being may have, from that [jewel] such [an object] appears accordingly.
Sentient beings perceive the sound issuing forth;

yet that great maṇi-jewel does not conceptualize, does not discriminate, does not think, and does not cogitate— it is inconceivable, free from thought, and devoid of mind, intellect, and consciousness.

In the same way, Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata does not conceptualize, does not discriminate, does not think, and does not reflect; he is beyond thought, free from thought, devoid of mind, intellect, and consciousness;
he is without grasping and without total appropriation.
He has not attained what is not to be attained;
he has cast off individualistic truths,
and he has cast off passion, cast off hatred, and cast off delusion.
Neither real nor false, neither permanent nor impermanent,
neither luminous nor non-luminous.
Neither world nor non-world, without applied thought or sustained thought, unarisen and unceasing.
Inconceivable and beyond thought, without intrinsic nature and devoid of the state of having an intrinsic nature,
empty of non-existence.
It is without taking up and without casting off; it is not to be adhered to;
it is beyond worldly discourse and the total cessation of worldly discourse.
Without joy, free from joy, the total eradication of delight;
unreckoned, beyond calculation;
without a path, going where there is no path, with all courses of existence utterly severed.
It is completely cut off from all verbal expression;
it is invisible, unobservable, and ungraspable;
it is neither space nor non-space.
It is neither visible nor demonstrable;
it is neither a collection nor a non-collection;
it is neither conceptualized nor non-conceptualized.
It is not established, not demonstrated,
undefiled, and not in need of purification;
it is neither name nor form nor sign.
There is neither karma nor the ripening of karma; it is neither past, nor future, nor present; it is devoid of anything whatsoever.
It is without conflict, without syllables, soundless, transcending all sound, and voiceless.
It is without characteristics, having transcended all characteristics;
it is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.
Nevertheless, Mañjuśrī, the jewel of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is purified by resolute intention and fixed upon the top of the banner of great compassion.
Then, whichever sentient being has an inclination according to their own disposition perceives the teaching of the Dharma issuing forth in that very way;
yet therein the Tathāgata is equal toward all, equanimous, free from conceptual construction, and without distinction.
Mañjuśrī, it is just as when beings perceive an echo issuing from the communication of another's voice;
yet that echo is neither past, nor future, nor present,
and it is not found internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.
Neither arisen nor ceased,
neither annihilated nor eternal,
neither possessing knowledge nor lacking knowledge.
Neither wisdom nor lack of wisdom, neither knowledge nor ignorance, neither liberation nor non-liberation.
It is neither blameworthy nor blameless, neither mindfulness nor lack of mindfulness,
neither possessing a basis nor lacking a basis.
Neither sitting nor not sitting;

neither the earth element, nor the water element, nor the fire element, nor the wind element; neither free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) nor accompanied by conceptual proliferation (*saprapañca*); nor...
It is sound, yet not sound; it is without syllables,
yet free from being without syllables.
It is soundless, transcending all sound; it is incomparable, transcending all comparison;
it is without characteristics, free from all characteristics.
Neither quiescence nor non-quiescence; neither long nor short; neither conscious nor unconscious.
Neither with a shrine nor without a shrine,
neither worldly nor unworldly, empty by its very nature of vision, it is non-recollection and non-mental-attention.
Without applied thought, without sustained thought,
and free from mind, intellect, and consciousness.
It is everywhere equal, non-conceptual, without distinction, and transcends the three times.
Nevertheless, Mañjuśrī, an echo issues forth from the perception of various sounds and voices according to the various inclinations of sentient beings, manifesting as diverse sounds and voices.
And those beings perceive them exactly in that way.
In the very same manner, Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is neither past, nor future, nor present;
he is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.
Neither arisen nor ceased,
neither annihilated nor eternal,
neither possessing knowledge nor lacking knowledge.
Neither possessing wisdom nor lacking wisdom, neither knowledge nor ignorance, neither liberation nor non-liberation.
Neither blameworthy nor blameless,
neither possessed of mindfulness nor lacking mindfulness,
neither possessing a fixed abode nor lacking a fixed abode.
Neither sitting nor not sitting;
neither the earth element, nor the water element, nor the fire element, nor the wind element; neither conceptual proliferation nor non-proliferation.
Neither sound nor non-sound, without syllables, voiceless, yet transcending all vocal expression.
Incomparable, having transcended all measure; without characteristics, free from characteristics;
neither peaceful nor unpeaceful.
Neither long nor short,
neither conscious nor unconscious, neither an object of thought nor not an object of thought.
Neither worldly nor non-worldly,
empty by its very nature of vision,
it is without recollection.
without mental attention, without applied thought, and without sustained thought;
It is free from mind, thought, and consciousness; it is equal toward all things, non-conceptual, without distinction, and transcends the three times.
Moreover, Mañjuśrī, sentient beings who are liberated in various ways perceive the voice of the Tathāgata as it issues forth according to their various inclinations and mental representations.
Mañjuśrī, it is just as all grasses, shrubs, medicinal herbs, and forest trees, depending upon the earth and established upon the earth, attain growth, development,
and abundance; yet, Mañjuśrī, the earth neither conceptualizes nor discriminates.

It is everywhere equal, non-conceptual, without distinction, free from thought, and devoid of mind, intellect, and consciousness. In just this way, Mañjuśrī, by relying upon the Tathāgata and being established in the Tathāgata, all the roots of merit of all sentient beings attain growth, development, and expansion.

Whether they belong to those of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the Mahāyāna, or to others such as the Carakas, Parivrājakas, Nirgranthas, and all other sectarian schools— even including the roots of goodness of those fixed in falsehood— all these roots of goodness, relying upon the Tathāgata and established in the Tathāgata, attain growth, increase, and expansion.
Moreover, Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata does not conceptualize and does not discriminate.
Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, has severed all conceptualization, discrimination, objective referents, and mental engagements.
It is free from mind, intellect, and consciousness; it is beyond reasoning and outside the sphere of reasoning.
unillumined,
inconceivable,
and beyond thought.
Without mental engagement,
free from anxiety,
and devoid of mind, intellect, and consciousness.
He is equal toward all, equanimous, free from conceptual construction, and without distinction.
Mañjuśrī, it is just as space is everywhere equal, free from conceptual construction, and without distinction;
unarisen and unceasing, neither past, nor future, nor present.
unobservable, free from conceptual proliferation, and indefinable.
invisible,
non-communicative, and intangible;
It is homeless,
incomparable, having transcended all measure; it is peerless, having transcended all analogy.
It is without foundation, ungraspable,
and beyond the range of the visual faculty.
It is free from mind, intellect, and consciousness; it is without characteristics and beyond syllables.
Soundless,
without mental engagement, without accumulation and without removal, without casting off and without adding.
It transcends the path of speech,
is omnipresent, and is non-abiding. Yet, Mañjuśrī, because sentient beings perceive forms as inferior, middling, or superior, they conceive of space as inferior or superior.
In the same way, Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is equal and without distinction everywhere;
he is unarisen and unceasing,
neither past, nor future, nor present.
It is uncharacterizable and free from conceptual proliferation;
it is formless, invisible, and non-cognizable; it is intangible and homeless.
Incomparable, having transcended all comparison; peerless, having transcended all analogy;
non-abiding.
Ungraspable,
transcending the path of the eye,
and free from mind, intellect, and consciousness.
It is without characteristics, without syllables, soundless, and without mental engagement.
Without exertion or withdrawal, without removal or addition,
it transcends the path of speech.
It follows and penetrates everywhere;
yet, Mañjuśrī, those beings who possess inferior, middling, or superior dispositions perceive the Tathāgata as inferior, middling, or superior.
Moreover, Mañjuśrī, it does not occur to the Tathāgata thus:
"This being is one whose resolute intention and inclination are inferior;
for this being, I shall manifest an inferior perfection of the form-body and its color."
This being is one whose inclination and resolve are middling;
I shall manifest to him a middling perfection of the color and form of the rūpakāya. This being is one whose inclination and resolve are sublime.
I shall demonstrate his magnificent perfection of the form-body's appearance.
In the same way, Mañjuśrī, it should be understood regarding the teaching of the Dharma.
And yet, Mañjuśrī, it does not occur to the Tathāgata:
"This one has inferior inclinations."
"This being has inferior aspirations; for this being, I shall deliver a discourse on the Śrāvaka vehicle.
This being is one whose inclination and resolve are middling; for this being, I shall deliver a discourse on the Pratyekabuddha vehicle."
This being is one whose resolve is inclined toward the noble intention;
for this being, I shall provide a discourse on the Mahāyāna.
Mañjuśrī, it does not occur to the Tathāgata in this way: "This being is one who is inclined toward the sublime; for this being, I shall deliver a discourse on generosity."
The same applies to ethical discipline, patience, vigor, and meditative concentration.
Mañjuśrī, it does not occur to the Tathāgata that "this sentient being is devoted to the perfection of wisdom."
"I shall speak the discourse on the perfection of wisdom for this being.
Mañjuśrī, it does not occur to the Tathāgata in such a way. Why is that?
Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata is the Dharmakāya;
Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata is absolutely unarisen.
Mañjuśrī, the consciousness of the Tathāgata does not proceed by following after names, forms, or verbal designations.
Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata does not conceptualize, nor does he discriminate.
For, Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata is momentary, characterized by inexhaustibility, and fixed upon the limit of the ultimate reality that is the limit of the inexhaustible.

Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha, reaches the limit of the equality of all phenomena; he is equal everywhere, free from conceptual construction, and without distinction—neither inferior, nor middling, nor superior.
In this very same way, Mañjuśrī, all phenomena are equal.
They are non-conceptual and without distinction;
they are neither inferior, nor middling, nor superior. For what reason?
Because all phenomena are non-apprehendable,
Mañjuśrī, that which is the non-apprehensibility of all phenomena is equality;
that which is equality is stability.
That which is stability is immovability; that which is immovability is non-reliance.
For one who is non-reliant upon all phenomena, there is no mental abiding.
For one whose mind does not abide, non-arising is produced.
And for one who sees thus, perverted mental states and mental factors do not arise.
And he whose mind is free from inversion has attained things as they truly are; one who has attained things as they truly are does not engage in conceptual proliferation.
For one who does not proliferate, there is no mental activity.
When it does not proceed, then it does not circulate;
when it does not circulate, then it does not disperse.
Not dispersing, it does not contradict the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Not contradicting the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one becomes compliant in all respects; being compliant in all respects, one does not deviate from the fundamental nature of phenomena (*dharmaprakṛti*);
not deviating from the fundamental nature of phenomena, one attains the fundamental nature of phenomena.
Having attained the fundamental nature of phenomena, one does not engage in any conceptual proliferation.
Why is that?
Because it is produced from causes and conditions.
That which is produced by causes and conditions is absolutely unborn;
and that which is absolutely unborn has attained the state of certainty.
And he who has attained the state of certainty does not dwell together with any mental engagements regarding phenomena (*dharmamanasikāra*).
When he does not dwell together with any mental engagements regarding phenomena, then he is no longer one who can cohabit.
When he is no longer one who can cohabit, then he neither comes into being nor passes away.

When one neither comes into being nor passes away, then one is established and has attained the Dharma. When one is established and has attained the Dharma, then one is engaged in the Dharma through proper application (*yoniśas*).
For one who is engaged in the Dharma through proper application, there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is not a Buddha-dharma.
For what reason?
Because of the realization of emptiness;
and that which is the realization of emptiness is awakening.
Thus, through the awakening to emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, lack of formative activity, homelessness, non-arising, ungraspability, and the absence of a substrate, there is awakening;
and awakening is right application.
It is proper application; by means of proper application, one is not abandoned. It is the absence of neglect and the absence of addition.
The application of forms and transformations,
the unconnected,
and the application that is not released.
The application of non-unity and non-diversity,
the application of the future, and the application of thoroughness.
Therein, there is no application, no means of valid cognition, and no direct realization of the fruit.
Why is that?
Because the mind is luminous by nature, and it is defiled by adventitious secondary afflictions; yet its nature is not defiled.
That which is natural luminosity is non-defilement;
and that which is non-defilement is such that no counteragent exists therein by which the abandonment of afflictions might occur.
For what reason?
One who is pure does not become purified; he is already pure.
That which is pure is non-arising;
that which is non-arising is irreproachable.
And that which is blameless is the abandonment of delight; therein all attachments cease.
Where all attachments cease, that is non-arising.
And that which is non-arising is awakening.
That which is awakening is equality;
that which is equality is suchness.
And all phenomena, both conditioned and unconditioned, are established in suchness.
That which is suchness (tathatā) is neither conditioned nor unconditioned, nor is it a designation of duality.
That wherein there is neither the conditioned nor the unconditioned, nor a designation of duality—that is suchness.
That which is suchness is non-other suchness.
That which is the suchness of non-duality is the suchness of immutability;
that which is the suchness of immutability is the suchness of the future;
and that which is the suchness of the future is the suchness of non-falsity.
That which is non-falsity is suchness as it truly is;
that which is suchness as it truly is is never-not-suchness;
that which is never-not-suchness is neither defiled nor purified.
That which is neither defiled nor purified does not arise and does not cease.
That which neither arises nor ceases is equal to nirvana.
That which is equal to nirvana neither wanders in samsara nor enters final nirvana.
That which neither transmigrates nor enters final nirvana is neither past, nor future, nor present.
That which is neither past, nor future, nor present is neither inferior, nor middling, nor superior.
That which is neither inferior, nor middling, nor superior is suchness.
That which is called "suchness" (tathatā) is a designation for the meaning of reality; it is called "reality" (tattva). Its state of being thus is called "suchness" (tathātva).
In the same way, suchness and the self are non-dual and indivisible;
and that which is the meaning of non-duality is awakening, in the sense of full comprehension.
"Meaning" is said to be the knowledge that enters the three gates of liberation regarding the teachings on all phenomena;
this is called "knowledge."
It is the entry into the equality of the three times regarding all phenomena;
it is called the "meaning" because it is the non-differentiated meaning of all phenomena.
It is soundless, inexpressible, beyond verbal discourse, and cut off from all discourse.
Knowledge is said to be that which follows after objects; furthermore, this knowledge is said to follow after consciousness. "Object" is said to be...
That which is the state of definitive meaning through the knowledge of the reality of things and the knowledge that follows from discernment—
that alone is the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā); and that which is the true nature of phenomena is the ultimate object (artha).

That true nature (*dharmatā*) is that which is understood through the knowledge that follows the meaning, the knowledge that follows the consciousness, and the knowledge that follows the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
That which is the true nature is the meaning; and that true nature is the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*) and the fixed order of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*).
That which does not proceed toward phenomena is the non-proceeding of phenomena;
and that which is the equality of meaning and phrasing is equal in the sense of non-duality.
That which is equality is the meaning;
that equality is through the knowledge of the meaning;
and that is the equality of knowledge by way of entering the door of non-duality.
The equality of the interpretable meaning with the definitive meaning is the same as that emptiness;
by virtue of being the same in meaning, the equality of persons is the same;
and by virtue of the equality of persons, the equality of phenomena is the same.
Through the equality of phenomena, the equality of liberation is equal;
and through the equality of liberation, awakening is the realization.
Mañjuśrī, for those joined with attachment to form, the eye is attachment;
the knowledge of the intrinsic nature of form and the eye is non-attachment.
For those joined with attachment to views, one's own body is attachment.
The knowledge of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of one's own body regarding all views that have been formed is non-attachment.
For those who are attached to the attachment of improper mental attention, the light of the Dharma is attachment;
whereas the knowledge of the emptiness of intrinsic nature and the emptiness of self-nature through the investigation of phenomena with proper mental attention is non-attachment.

For those attached to the stain of doubt, liberation is attachment; for those [possessing] resolute belief, liberation, and knowledge of reality as it is, non-attachment is [liberation]. For those attached to the stain of laziness, the attainment of vigor through seeing [the truth] is attachment.
The awakening to phenomena as they are is non-attachment; for those possessed of attachment to the hindrances, the factors of enlightenment are non-attachment;
the liberation of unobstructed knowledge is non-attachment.
All phenomena are pure by nature; they proceed through the assembly of causes and conditions.
In this regard, a bodhisattva must thoroughly understand both the cause of affliction and the cause of purification.
Furthermore, one should not abide in either the purification of the cause of affliction or the purification of the cause of purification.
The arising of a self is the cause of affliction;
the patient acceptance that enters into the dharma of selflessness is the cause of purification;
and the view of "I" and "mine" is the cause of affliction.
Inner tranquility and the absence of outward activity are the causes of purification;
whereas discursive thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, and cruelty are the causes of affliction.

The patience that enters into the dharma of dependent origination—consisting of the contemplations on impurity, loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—is the cause of purification.
The four perversions are the cause of affliction;
the four foundations of mindfulness are the cause of purification.
The five hindrances are the cause of affliction;
the five faculties are the cause of purification;
the six sense bases are the cause of affliction.
The six recollections are the cause of purification;
the seven non-virtuous factors are the cause of affliction;
the seven factors of enlightenment are the cause of purification.
The eight types of wrongness are the cause of affliction;
the eight types of rightness are the cause of purification;
and the nine bases of malice are the cause of affliction.
The nine successive attainments of meditative abiding are the cause of purification;
the ten unwholesome paths of action are the cause of affliction;
and the ten wholesome paths of action are the cause of purification.
In brief, all unwholesome mental engagements are the cause of affliction,
and all wholesome mental engagements are the cause of purification.

In this regard, whatever is the cause of affliction and whatever is the cause of purification—all those phenomena are empty by nature; they are without a sentient being, without a life-principle, without a nourisher, without a person, and without an individual; they are without an owner, without possession, and without activity; they are like an illusion, without characteristics, and inwardly peaceful.
That which is internal tranquility is peace;
that which is peace is the fundamental nature;
that which is the fundamental nature is non-apprehension.
That which is non-apprehension is without abode; that which is without abode is space;
and space is the sky.
He understands all phenomena to be equal to space;
he engages in the conventions of affliction and purification,
yet he does not abandon the nature of space.
For what reason?
Mañjuśrī, there exists no phenomenon whatsoever for which there could be either arising or cessation.
"In that case, Blessed One, how was awakening attained by the Tathāgata?
The Blessed One said:
"Mañjuśrī, awakening was attained by the Tathāgata as being rootless and without foundation."
"In that regard, Blessed One, what is the root and what is the foundation?
The Blessed One said:
"Mañjuśrī, the root is the view of a self-identity (*satkāya*), and the foundation is unreal conceptualization (*abhūtaparikalpa*)."
Mañjuśrī, by means of the equality of awakening, the Tathāgata has known the equality of all phenomena;
therefore, Mañjuśrī, it is said that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to an awakening that is rootless and without foundation.
Mañjuśrī, awakening is peaceful and thoroughly pacified.
In that regard, what is peace and what is thorough pacification?
Peace is internal tranquility.
There is external tranquility. For what reason?
Mañjuśrī, the eye is empty of a self and of what belongs to a self.
This is its very nature;
this is called tranquility (*śama*).
Having thoroughly understood that the eye is empty, one does not run after forms.
Therefore, it is called "quiescence.
Likewise, the ear is empty of a self and of what belongs to a self;
such is its intrinsic nature.
This is called tranquility (*śama*).
Having fully understood that the ear is empty, one does not run after sounds;
therefore, it is called pacification (*upaśama*).
The nose is empty of a self and of what belongs to a self;
such is its nature.
This is called tranquility.
Having thoroughly understood that the nose is empty, one does not run after odors; therefore, it is called "quiescence.
The tongue is empty of self and of what belongs to a self.
This is its very nature;
this is called tranquility (*śama*).
Having fully understood that the tongue is empty, one does not [cling] to tastes.
It flows; therefore it is called "quiescence.
The body is empty of a self and of what belongs to a self;
such is its very nature.
This is called tranquility (*śama*).
Having fully understood that the body is empty, one does not run toward tangible objects;
therefore, it is called pacification (*upaśama*).
“Mañjuśrī, the mind is empty of self and of what belongs to a self; this is its very nature. This is called ‘peace.’”
Having fully understood that the mind is empty, one does not run after phenomena;
therefore, it is called "quiescence."
Mañjuśrī, awakening is luminous by nature because the nature of the mind is luminous; for that reason, it is called "luminous by nature. That which is its nature is undefiled.
Equal to space,
having the nature of space,
and converging into space.
The nature is like space, absolutely luminous.
“Mañjuśrī, awakening is without acquisition and without relinquishment.
In that regard, what is non-acquisition and what is non-relinquishment? It is called ‘non-acquisition’ because there is no grasping at any phenomena.”
"Non-removal" is said to be the non-abandonment of all phenomena.
In this regard, Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata has crossed the flood by means of neither bringing in nor removing;
he has crossed it in such a way that he perceives neither the near shore nor the far shore within suchness.
For thus have all dharmas, which are devoid of both the near and the far shores, been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata;
therefore he is called the "Tathāgata."
“Mañjuśrī, awakening is signless and objectless.
In that regard, what is signlessness and what is objectlessness? Mañjuśrī, the non-apprehension of visual consciousness is signlessness.”
The non-observation of form is non-objectification;
the non-apprehension of auditory consciousness is signlessness;
the non-hearing of sounds is non-objectification.
The non-apprehension of olfactory consciousness is signlessness;
the non-olfaction of odors is objectlessness.
The non-apprehension of gustatory consciousness is signlessness.
The non-apprehension of the tasting of flavors is objectlessness;
the non-perception of body-consciousness is signlessness;
the non-touching of tangible objects is objectlessness.
The non-apprehension of mental consciousness is signlessness;
the non-cognition of phenomena is objectlessness.
Mañjuśrī, this is the sphere of activity of the noble ones.
That which is not the domain within the triple world,
Mañjuśrī, this is the domain of the noble ones.
“Mañjuśrī, awakening is neither past, nor future, nor present; it is equal throughout the three times and delimited by the three spheres.
In this regard, Mañjuśrī, what is the delimitation of the three spheres?
It is that the mind is not apprehended in the past.”
Consciousness does not run toward the future;
mental attention does not operate in the present.
Not established in mind, mentation, or consciousness, he neither conceptualizes nor discriminates.
Not conceiving and not discriminating, one does not construct the past, does not imagine the future, and does not proliferate conceptual elaborations regarding the present.
“Mañjuśrī, awakening is bodiless and unconditioned.
In this regard, Mañjuśrī, its bodilessness is that which is not cognizable by visual consciousness,
nor by auditory [consciousness],” and so forth.
It is not perceived by the nose, nor by the tongue,
nor by mental consciousness.
Mañjuśrī, that which is not to be cognized by mind, intellect, or consciousness is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
That which is called unconditioned is where there is no arising, no abiding, and no passing away.
That is called the unconditioned purified of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍalapariśuddha*).
Just as the unconditioned is, so too should the conditioned be understood.
For what reason? Because whatever is the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, that is a non-intrinsic nature.
In that regard, there is no duality.
“Mañjuśrī, awakening is an indivisible term. In that regard, what is the indivisibility, and what is the term?”
The non-differentiation of non-conception is suchness;
the station is the non-abiding, the non-differentiation, the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
The non-differentiation of non-diversity is the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi); it is the station.
Non-apprehension is non-differentiation; immovability is the state.
Non-differentiation from emptiness is the signless state.
Absence of discursive thought is non-differentiation; the wishless is the state.
The absence of longing is non-differentiation; the state is the absence of sentient beings.
The absence of intrinsic nature in sentient beings is non-differentiation; the state is space.
Non-apprehension is non-differentiation; the state is non-arising.
Non-cessation and non-differentiation is the unconditioned state; non-activity and non-differentiation is awakening as the state;
quiescence and non-differentiation is nirvana as the state.
Non-origination, non-differentiation, and non-birth are the state.
“Mañjuśrī, awakening is not fully realized by means of the body, nor by means of the mind.
For what reason?
Mañjuśrī, the body is insentient, inactive, and devoid of consciousness; it is like grass, wood, a wall, a clod of earth, or a reflection.”
The mind, Mañjuśrī, is like an illusion— empty, hollow, unreal, and unconditioned.
Mañjuśrī, this kind of realization regarding both the body and the mind is called awakening.
This is based on conventional usage, but not from the perspective of ultimate reality.
For what reason?
Mañjuśrī, awakening cannot be described as being by means of body, mind, dharma, or non-dharma; nor as real or unreal, nor as true or false.
“Mañjuśrī, awakening is inexpressible by means of all phenomena.
Why is that?
Because, Mañjuśrī, awakening is not some location by which it could enter into conventional discourse.”

Mañjuśrī, just as the locus of space is unconditioned, unarisen, unceasing, and inexpressible, so too, Mañjuśrī, awakening (bodhi) is unconditioned, without locus, unarisen, unceasing, and inexpressible. Mañjuśrī, just as reality (bhūta), when thoroughly sought,
is inexpressible by means of all phenomena, even so, Mañjuśrī, awakening— reality itself— when thoroughly sought, is inexpressible by means of all phenomena.
For what reason?
Mañjuśrī, speech does not exist in reality, because it is neither produced nor ceased.
“Mañjuśrī, awakening is non-apprehensibility and non-abiding.
In this regard, Mañjuśrī, what is non-apprehensibility and what is non-abiding? Mañjuśrī, the thorough knowledge of the eye is non-apprehensibility; the non-perception of forms is non-abiding.”
The non-apprehensibility of sound through the thorough knowledge of the ear is non-abiding; the non-apprehensibility of odor through the thorough knowledge of the nose is non-abiding;
the non-apprehensibility of taste through the thorough knowledge of the tongue is non-abiding.
The thorough knowledge of the body is non-apprehensibility; it is the non-perception of the tangible and the state of being without a substrate.
The thorough knowledge of the mind is non-apprehensibility; it is the non-perception of phenomena and the state of being without a substrate.

Thus has the Tathāgata fully awakened to enlightenment, which is ungraspable and without abode. Having fully awakened, because there is no apprehension of form, visual consciousness does not abide for the sake of favoring the eye; because there is no apprehension of sound, auditory consciousness does not abide for the sake of favoring the ear.
Because there is no apprehension of odors due to the non-benefiting of the nose, olfactory consciousness is not established;
because there is no apprehension of tastes due to the non-benefiting of the tongue, gustatory consciousness is not established;
and because there is no apprehension of tangibles due to the non-benefiting of the body.
Body-consciousness is not established.
Because the mind does not find support and because phenomena are not apprehended, mental consciousness is not established.
Therefore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha, is designated as one whose consciousness is non-abiding.
Mañjuśrī, there are these four bases for the minds of sentient beings.
What are the four? Namely, form is a basis for the minds of sentient beings;
likewise, feeling, perception, and mental formations, Mañjuśrī, are bases for the minds of sentient beings.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, these four foundations of the mind have been known by the Tathāgata as neither arisen nor ceased.
“Awakening,” Mañjuśrī, is a designation for emptiness.
By that very emptiness through which awakening is empty, Mañjuśrī, all phenomena are empty.
Just as they are empty, so have they been perfectly awakened to by the Tathāgata.
Mañjuśrī, emptiness is not fully awakened to by means of emptiness.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, this is a single principle, namely, emptiness or awakening.
Where, Mañjuśrī, there is neither emptiness nor awakening, [that is the ultimate reality].
In that regard, Mañjuśrī, there is no duality whatsoever by which emptiness or awakening could be made into two.
Why is that?
Mañjuśrī, all phenomena are non-dual, without characteristics, without division, nameless, signless, free from mind, thought, and consciousness, unarisen, and unceasing.
They are without conduct, without movement, without manifestation, without letters, and without sound.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, that which is called "empty" is a designation for the absence of grasping through attachment;
yet, Mañjuśrī, in this ultimate sense, no phenomenon whatsoever is apprehended that could be called "empty."
Just as, Mañjuśrī, space is called "space," yet space is inexpressible;
even so, Mañjuśrī, emptiness is called "emptiness."
The entry into all phenomena is into that which is ineffable and empty.
Mañjuśrī, all phenomena are nameless, and yet they are designated by names.
Mañjuśrī, a name does not abide in a location, nor does it abide in a particular place.

Just as they were perfectly awakened to by the Tathāgata, even that dharma which is expressed by name does not abide in a location, nor does it abide in a specific place. Thus, Mañjuśrī, all these dharmas have been known by the Tathāgata from the very beginning as unborn, unarisen, unceasing, without characteristics, free from mind, thought, and consciousness, and beyond letters and sounds.
Just as they are known, so too are they resolved upon;
Mañjuśrī, the Buddha does not resolve upon anything.
Mañjuśrī, awakening is equal to space;
and as space is neither equal nor unequal,
so too awakening is neither equal nor unequal.
For what reason?
Mañjuśrī, that dharma which has no real perfection cannot be said to be either equal or unequal.
Indeed, Mañjuśrī, all dharmas have been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata as neither equal nor unequal.
And thus, having attained perfect awakening, not even an atom was made equal or made unequal;
those phenomena were understood exactly as they are. And what, Mañjuśrī, is this knowledge of reality? It is that all phenomena are unarisen and unceasing.
Having not existed, they come to be; and having existed, they pass away.
And these arise without an owner and without being grasped.
Mañjuśrī, they pass away ownerless and without grasping.
Thus, Mañjuśrī, things arise and cease in dependence upon conditions; they proceed according to the nature of phenomena (dharma), yet there is no agent who causes them to proceed.
Therefore it is said that the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma for the sake of cutting off [the notion of] phenomena.

"Enlightenment," Mañjuśrī, is this term for things as they truly are. In that regard, Mañjuśrī, what is the term for things as they truly are? Mañjuśrī, enlightenment— [...is] the term for things as they truly are. What, Mañjuśrī, is the term for things as they truly are? Mañjuśrī, enlightenment is the term for things as they truly are."
As is awakening, so is form; it does not transcend suchness.
As is awakening, so are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; they do not transcend suchness.
As is awakening, so is the earth element; it does not transcend suchness.
Just as awakening is, so too the water element and the fire element do not deviate from suchness.
Just as awakening is, so too the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element do not deviate from suchness.
For just as awakening is, Mañjuśrī, so too the ear element, the sound element, and the ear-consciousness element [do not deviate from suchness].
The nose element, the odor element, and the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element;
the body element, the tangible object element, and the body-consciousness element.
The mind-element, the dharma-element, and the mind-consciousness-element do not transcend suchness. This designation of phenomena is limited to this extent:
namely, the designation of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields.
That has been perfectly awakened to by the Tathāgata as it truly is: just as it is before, so it is after, and so it is in the middle;
unarisen from the past limit, non-transmigrating to the future limit, and secluded in the middle.
In this very way, their state of being as it truly is comes to be.
As it is with one, so it is with all;
as it is with all, so it is with one.
And herein, Mañjuśrī, neither unity nor plurality is perceived.
“Mañjuśrī, awakening enters by way of form, yet it has entered into the absence of form.
In this regard, Mañjuśrī, what is form? And what is the absence of form?”
Mañjuśrī, "aspect" (ākāra) is said to be the undertaking of all wholesome phenomena;
"non-aspect" (anākāra) is said to be the non-apprehension of all phenomena. "Aspect" is said to be the stabilization of the unsettled mind.
The signless concentration, which is a gateway to liberation, is called "formless" (anākāra).
"Form" (ākāra) refers to the liberation consisting of the mind's weighing, measuring, counting, and discerning all phenomena.
The "formless" (anākāra) is said to be the transcendence of the scale.
And what is the transcendence of the scale?
It is that wherein there is no activity of consciousness.
"Aspect" refers to the contemplation of the conditioned;
"non-aspect" refers to the contemplation of the unconditioned.
“Mañjuśrī, awakening is the state of being without outflows and without grasping.
In this regard, Mañjuśrī, what is ‘without outflows’ and what is ‘without grasping’?
Mañjuśrī, the state of being without outflows is said to be the departure from the four outflows.”
Of which four?
Namely, the outflow of sensual desire,
the outflow of existence, and so forth.
Of the outflow of ignorance, of the outflow of views,
and of these four outflows.
Non-clinging is said to be the cessation of the four types of clinging.
Which four?
Clinging to sensual desire, [clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, and clinging to a doctrine of self].
of the clinging to views,
the clinging to rules and observances,
and the clinging to the doctrine of self.
Of these four types of clinging,
all are blinded by ignorance and made restless by craving.
They are grasped through mutual attachment.
In this regard, Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata has thoroughly understood the root of the grasping of the doctrine of self;
through the purity of the self, he has realized the purity of all sentient beings.
That which is the purity of the self is the purity of all sentient beings;
that which is the purity of all sentient beings is non-dual and without differentiation;
and that which is the meaning of non-duality is neither arising nor ceasing.
Mañjuśrī, in the absence of arising and cessation, mind, intellect, and consciousness do not function;
therein there is no conceptual construction by which one might engage in improper mental attention through discrimination.

One who engages in appropriate mental attention does not give rise to ignorance; and that non-arising of ignorance is the non-arising of the twelve links of existence. That non-arising of the twelve links of existence is birthlessness.
That which is non-arising is the fixed course;
that which is the fixed course is the definitive meaning;
that which is the definitive meaning is the ultimate truth.
That which is the ultimate meaning is the meaning of the absence of a person; that which is the meaning of the absence of a person is the inexpressible meaning;
and that which is the inexpressible meaning is the meaning of dependent origination.
That which is the meaning of dependent origination is the meaning of the Dharma;
that which is the meaning of the Dharma is the meaning of the Tathāgata. Therefore it is said:
He who sees dependent origination sees the Dharma;
he who sees the Dharma sees the Tathāgata.
And he sees in such a way that, when thoroughly investigated, he sees nothing at all.
In that regard, Mañjuśrī, what is "something"?
It is namely the mind and its object.
When there is neither mind—
And when one does not perceive an object, then one perceives reality;
in this way, these phenomena have been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata as equal through their sameness.
“Mañjuśrī, awakening is pure, stainless, and free from defilement.
In this regard, Mañjuśrī, what is purity? What is the stainless?”
What is freedom from blemish?
Mañjuśrī, emptiness is purity;
the signless is stainlessness.
The wishless is freedom from defilement;
non-arising is purity,
and the absence of formative activity is stainlessness.
Non-arising is the absence of defilement;
intrinsic nature is purity,
and complete purification is stainlessness.
Luminosity is the absence of blemish;
non-proliferation is purity, and being free from proliferation is stainlessness.
The subsiding of conceptual proliferation is the absence of affliction;
suchness is purity,
and the realm of phenomena is stainless.
The limit of reality is without blemish;
space is purity,
and the sky is stainless.
Patience is freedom from blemish; internal purity is the absence of outward wandering, which is stainlessness.
Non-apprehension both internally and externally is freedom from defilement;
thorough knowledge of the aggregates is purity;
the intrinsic nature of the elements is stainlessness.
The removal of the sense bases is freedom from affliction;
regarding the past, the knowledge of destruction is purity;
regarding the future, the knowledge of non-arising is stainlessness.
"In the present, there is the knowledge of abiding in the dharma-realm, which is free from defilement.
Thus, Mañjuśrī, purity, stainlessness, and freedom from defilement converge in a single state;
that is to say, in the state of peace.
That which is calm is thoroughly calmed; that which is thoroughly calmed is completely stilled;
that which is completely stilled is peace.
And that which is tranquility is called a sage.
Thus, Mañjuśrī, as is space, so is awakening;
as is awakening, so are all phenomena.
As are phenomena, so are sentient beings;
as are sentient beings, so are fields;
as are fields, so is nirvana.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī, it is said that all phenomena are equal to nirvāṇa;
they are without counteragent in the cause that is the ultimate limit,
and by virtue of having no counteragent as their cause, they are primordially pure.
They are primordially pure and primordially stainless.
