In that regard, Mañjuśrī, for the Tathāgata who has thus fully awakened to all phenomena as being of such a nature, [the state] of sentient beings—
And as he contemplates the realm [of sentient beings],
there arises toward them a great compassion called "the Playful," which is pure, stainless, and free from defilement.
How, Mañjuśrī, does a bodhisattva practice the bodhisattva course?

When, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva does not conceive of things in terms of destruction or arising, nor in terms of non-destruction or non-arising, nor as anything other than the exhaustion of what is exhausted,
and does not disturb the state of ultimate non-arising.
And thus, Mañjuśrī, does one practice the bodhisattva conduct.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva does not practice with the thought that the past mind has perished,
nor does he practice with the thought that the future mind has not yet arrived.
He does not course in the thought that the present mind is stationary;
nor does he become attached to past, future, or present minds.
Coursing in this way, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva courses in the bodhisattva practice.
“Mañjuśrī, generosity, awakening, sentient beings, and the Tathāgata—these are non-dual and not divided into two.
Practicing in this way, a bodhisattva practices the conduct of a bodhisattva.
Mañjuśrī, ethical discipline, awakening, sentient beings, and the Tathāgata—these are non-dual and not divided into two.”
Practicing in this way, a bodhisattva practices the bodhisattva course.
In this way, patience is awakening, sentient beings, and the Tathāgata;
diligence is awakening, sentient beings, and the Tathāgata.
Meditative concentration, awakening, sentient beings, and the Tathāgata—likewise, wisdom, awakening, the Tathāgata, and sentient beings: these are non-dual and undivided.
Mañjuśrī, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva practices the conduct of a bodhisattva.
If, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva does not course in the thought that "form is empty," nor that "it is not empty"—
coursing thus, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva courses in the bodhisattva practice.
For what reason?
Form itself is empty of the intrinsic nature of form;
likewise, he practices with the thought that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, and not non-empty.
Practicing in this way, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva practices the bodhisattva course.
For what reason?
Because mind, intellect, and consciousness are not apprehended.
Mañjuśrī, there exists no such dharma whatsoever.
Mañjuśrī, that which one would fully understand, or abandon, or cultivate, or realize— that which is awakened to—
is "exhaustion"; it is indeed the ultimate exhaustion.
And that which is already utterly exhausted is not to be further exhausted; it is inexhaustible because it is the exhaustion of the inexhaustible. For what reason?
And as for that exhaustion:
that which is exhaustion as it truly is is the exhaustion of nothing whatsoever.
That which is the exhaustion of nothing whatsoever is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
That which is unconditioned has neither arising nor cessation. Therefore it is said:
whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the stability of phenomena (dharmasthititā), and the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) remain ever established.

Just as the abiding of the *dharmadhātu* is such that the wisdom of the Tathāgata neither proceeds nor ceases, so too, through entry into this method of Dharma, the outflows (*āsrava*) are neither produced nor extinguished.
Mañjuśrī, "the destruction of the outflows" is merely a conventional expression, a sound, a syllable, a sign, and a designation; herein no phenomenon whatsoever is produced or extinguished.

Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, praised the Blessed One with these verses:
Without color, mark, or shape; without cessation, without origination; rootless, without foundation, and without support—homage be to you!
Without abiding, without drawing in, without pushing out, and without remaining;
liberated from the six sense bases and without support—homage be to you!
Not abiding in any phenomena, free from existence and non-existence,
having attained the equality of conditioned things— homage be to you, O supportless one!
Liberated from the three realms, you have attained equality with space;
you are unstained by desires, O supportless one—homage be to you!
You are always in a state of meditative equipoise, whether walking, standing, or even lying down;
in all modes of conduct, O supportless one, homage be to you!
You abide equally, you move equally, established in equanimity;
you do not disturb equanimity. O supportless one, homage be to you!
Having attained equanimity, you are concentrated in all phenomena;
having entered the signless, you are without support—homage be to you!
Unestablished, without support, and concentrated in the peak of wisdom; having attained mastery over all phenomena, O Unsupported One, homage be to you!
Homage be to you, O Non-referential One, who in a single instant teaches all the forms, sounds, and postures of all sentient beings.
Freed from name and form, having severed the causes of the aggregates, you have entered the formless; O supportless one, homage be to you!
You have departed from signs and are free from the activity of signs;
you have entered the signless, O supportless one—homage be to you!
O you whose intentions are free from conceptualization, whose mind is non-abiding,
who are without recollection or mental engagement, and who are without support— homage be to you!
Without abode like space, free from conceptual proliferation, and stainless;
you possess a mind equal to space, O supportless one—homage be to you!
Space is without end or middle, and such is the very nature of the Buddhas;
you who transcend the three times and are without support—to you, I pay homage.
The Buddhas have the characteristic of space, and space is also without characteristics;
free from cause and effect, without support—homage be to you!
Ungraspable like the moon in water, not dependent on any phenomena,
without egoism, without sound, and without support— homage be to you!
You are not dependent upon the aggregates, the elements, or the sense-bases;
liberated from all perversions and without any point of reference, homage be to you!
Free from the two extremes, having utterly uprooted the view of a self, you have attained the equality of the dharmadhātu; O you who are without support, homage be to you!
Free from the enumeration of form, devoid of non-existent phenomena, without grasping, without relinquishing, and without support— homage be to you!
Having transcended the faults of Māra, you have reached the goal of the realm of phenomena;
you possess the unobstructed Dharma—homage be to you, O supportless one!
Those who know the true meaning do not say "it exists," nor do they say "it does not exist.
You are beyond the path of speech, ungraspable, and without support; homage be to you!
Not relying on the duality of phenomena, you have utterly severed the banner of pride;
liberated from both duality and non-duality, O Supportless One, homage be to you!
The mental defects and the fourfold physical ones have been conquered by you;
O inconceivable one, beyond comparison, without support, homage be to you!
You act without effort, being entirely free from all faults; your activity is preceded by wisdom. O you who are without support, homage be to you!
Your mindfulness is untainted, subtle, and absorbed in both the real and the unreal; you are homeless, free from conceptual construction, and without support—homage be to you!
With a mind that has no object of reference, you understand all minds;
you have no perception of self or other, being without support—homage be to you!
Without object and without support, you are the deluder of all minds;
you are the dharma that is without object. O you who are without support, homage be to you!
That mind is without an object and does not exist by way of its own nature;
O inconceivable one who has attained equanimity, who is without support, homage be to you!
With non-reliant gnosis you behold all buddha-fields and the conduct of all sentient beings; O you who are without support, homage be to you!
The mind has never been apprehended by the Buddhas in any way whatsoever;
O Omniscient One, you for whom all phenomena are without objective support—homage be to you!
All phenomena are like an illusion, and yet the illusion itself does not exist;
O you who are free from illusory phenomena and without support, homage be to you!
O Perfectly Awakened One, you move through the world unattached to worldly phenomena; you do not conceptualize the world. O You who are without support, homage be to you!
You move in emptiness because of emptiness; because of emptiness, your sphere of activity is empty.
You declare that even emptiness is empty. O you who are without support, homage be to you!
You manifest through great supernatural power by means of the illusion-like samādhi;
having attained the state of non-differentiation, O you who are without support, homage be to you!
You do not abide in multiplicity or diversity, nor in the distant or the near;
you are without lifting up or casting down, without support—homage be to you!
Awakened in a single instant by the diamond-like samādhi, you have entered the state of non-appearance; O you who are without support, homage be to you!
O Leader, you know the immovable Nirvana throughout all three times;
endowed with diverse skillful means, O supportless one, homage be to you!
Skilled in the knowledge of means for the sake of sentient beings through successive transmission, you realize the immovable Nirvana; O you who are without support, homage be to you!
Homage be to you, who are signless, effortless, free from conceptual proliferation, and free from affliction; who are without appearance, the unique selflessness, and without support.
O Omniscient One, you who are free from conceptual construction and devoid of "mine-ness," just as you know the self by yourself, so too are you everywhere without support; homage be to you!
I pay homage to you, O One of Ten Powers, who have crossed over the flood; I pay homage to you, the fearless giver of fearlessness;
I pay homage to you, who have attained certainty in the unique qualities of the Dharma; I pay homage to you, the leader of the entire world.
I pay homage to you, the cutter of the bonds of fetters; I pay homage to you, who have gone to the further shore and stand firm upon it.
I pay homage to you, the leader of the wearying world; I pay homage to you, who have entered saṃsāra yet remain unattached.
I pay homage to you, O Sage, who are free from the concentration on sentient beings, whose mind is liberated in all births and states of existence;
like a lotus in the water, you are not defiled by the waters, for you, O Buddha, have cultivated emptiness.
I pay homage to the unsurpassed state of the Teacher, which is characterized by solitude, is without support, and has crossed over the great flood;
you have completely analyzed all signs in every way, and no aspiration whatsoever exists for you.
I pay homage to the Buddha’s inconceivable and great majesty, which is equal to space and independent;
I pay homage to you, the bearer of all supreme qualities; I pay homage to you, whose glory rises high like Mount Meru.
Then the Blessed One gave his approval to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!
Well spoken by you, Mañjuśrī; it is just so."
Mañjuśrī, Buddhas are not to be seen by way of form, nor by way of phenomena, nor by way of characteristics, nor by way of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Buddhas are neither solitary nor situated in the midst of a great multitude.
Buddhas have not been seen by anyone.
They have not been heard, nor have they been honored, nor are they being honored.
Buddhas do not effect the oneness or the multiplicity of any dharma.
Enlightenment has not been attained by Buddhas.
The Buddhas are not characterized by any dharma whatsoever;
no dharma has been seen, heard, remembered, cognized, or known by the Buddhas;
nothing has been spoken or uttered by the Buddhas.
The Buddhas do not speak, they do not utter;
the Buddhas will not speak, they will not utter;
the Buddhas do not fully awaken.
No dharma has been fully awakened to by the Buddhas;
no afflictions have been abandoned by the Buddhas, nor has purification been realized.
No dharma whatsoever has been seen by the Buddhas, nor heard, nor smelled, nor cognized. For what reason?
Because all phenomena are pure from the very beginning.

Mañjuśrī, suppose there were a certain bodhisattva who established as many sentient beings as there are atoms in a trichiliocosm mahāsāhasra world-system in the state of a pratyekabuddha, yet lacked faith in this Dharma discourse;
and suppose, Mañjuśrī, there were another bodhisattva who had faith in this Dharma discourse. [The latter would generate far more merit than the former.]
This person generates much more merit than that;
how much more so, then, for one who would write down this Dharma-discourse or cause it to be written?
This very person generates even greater merit than that.
Mañjuśrī, as many beings as there are found in the triple-thousand great-thousand world system— whether born from a womb or born from moisture—
whether they are of spontaneous birth,
or possessed of perception, or devoid of perception;
Whether they be footless, or two-footed,
or four-footed;
Or even those with many feet—
all of them, by virtue of conceptual construction,
might obtain a human existence that is neither prior nor subsequent.

Having obtained a human body, they should generate the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*). Having generated the thought of awakening, may each individual bodhisattva serve Buddhas and bodhisattvas— as numerous as the atoms in Buddha-fields equal to the sands of the Ganges—
along with their disciples, providing them with robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
One should provide all the requisites for happiness and,
for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges,
one should construct stupas for those who have attained parinirvāṇa.
They were made of jewels, rising a hundred yojanas high, and surrounded by jeweled railings.
They were beautified with garlands of jewels, pearls, and gems; with parasols, banners, and flags raised aloft;
and covered by a net of *vaśirāja* jewel-gems.
And if another bodhisattva, endowed with pure intention,
having heard this Dharma discourse— the Ornament of the Light of Wisdom for Entering the Domain of All Buddhas— should have faith in it, enter into it, believe it, and master it,
or should at least recite a single verse, he would generate incalculably more merit than that.
The pursuit of the Buddha’s wisdom is conducive to this formation of merit;
compared to this formation of merit, that previous formation of merit—
the bodhisattvas’ basis of meritorious action consisting of giving— does not approach even a hundredth part of it.
Even a thousandth part,
even a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part,
even a mere fraction.
It does not admit of calculation, nor comparison, nor even a fraction thereof.

Mañjuśrī, suppose some householder bodhisattva were to attend upon as many Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and their assemblies of śrāvakas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, providing them with robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick; and suppose another bodhisattva who has gone forth, being virtuous and endowed with pure intention, were to give even a single morsel of food to a single sentient being, even one belonging to the animal realm. [The latter would generate far more merit than the former.]
Compared to that formation of merit, the previous formation of merit does not approach even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part.
Not even a thousandth part of ten million billion,
nor even a fraction as small as a comparison (upaniṣad), can bear it.
Mañjuśrī, suppose there were as many bodhisattvas who have gone forth, possessed of ethical discipline and pure intention, as there are atoms in a great trichiliocosm;

and suppose each one of those bodhisattvas were to provide robes, alms-food, bedding, seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick to as many Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and their assemblies of disciples as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, for as many incalculable eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.
Whatever accumulation of merit consisting of giving those bodhisattvas might have,
or whatever other bodhisattva— whether a layperson or one who has gone forth— who, being pure in intention and possessed of ethical discipline,
having heard this Dharma-discourse, should have faith in it or accept it, or write it down or cause it to be written; [the latter’s merit would be greater].
Compared to this accumulation of merit, that previous accumulation of merit— the basis of meritorious action consisting of the gift of those bodhisattvas— does not approach even a hundredth part,
nor even a thousandth part.
It does not admit even a fraction of a comparison.

Mañjuśrī, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to fill the great trichiliocosm with the seven precious jewels and give it as a gift to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— and if, giving in this manner, he were to give such gifts for as many eons as there are atoms in a great trichiliocosm; yet another bodhisattva were to teach these Dharma-discourses, even if only a single four-line verse, to a bodhisattva.
That former accumulation of merit does not approach even a hundredth part of this accumulation of merit, nor a thousandth part,
nor even a hundred-thousandth part.
It does not admit even a hundred-thousandth part, nor even a fraction, nor even a comparison (upaniṣad).
"Mañjuśrī, let alone the accumulation of merit from one who gives gifts for as many eons as there are atoms in a great trichiliocosm world-system.
Suppose, Mañjuśrī, there were as many bodhisattvas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges;
and suppose each single bodhisattva [were to fill] with Jāmbūnada gold as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges."
Having wrapped all the trees with divine garments,
having covered them with nets of *sarvaprabhāsamuccaya* jewel-gems,
and having filled them with gabled pavilions made of *vaśirāja* jewel-gems, surrounded by railings of *vidyutpradīpa* jewel-gems;

If one were to offer gifts day after day to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, with parasols, banners, and flags raised high— and if one were to continue giving in this manner for as many eons as there are sands in the river Ganges—

yet another Bodhisattva, having gained faith in this Dharma-discourse, were to teach or introduce even a single four-line stanza from this Dharma-discourse to another Bodhisattva; [the latter would generate greater merit].
Compared to this accumulation of merit, that previous accumulation of merit consisting of the gift-giving of those bodhisattvas does not approach even a hundredth part,
nor a thousandth part,
nor even a hundred-thousandth part.
Even as a number, even as a fraction, even as a calculation, [it cannot be compared].
It does not even come within the range of secondary similes, nor even within the range of a primary simile.
Mañjuśrī, it is as if all sentient beings included within the three realms—those born in the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the world of Yama—were to exist;
and then a householder bodhisattva were to rescue them all from the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the world of Yama, and establish them in the state of a pratyekabuddha.
Yet, another bodhisattva who has gone forth into homelessness might give even a single morsel of food to a being belonging to the animal realm. [The latter would generate far greater merit.]
This person would generate much more merit, indeed an incalculably greater merit than that.
Mañjuśrī, suppose there were renunciant bodhisattvas in the ten directions as numerous as the atoms in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of inexpressible Buddha-fields;

and suppose that each one of those bodhisattvas were to see Buddhas, Blessed Ones, in every single direction throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the atoms in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of inexpressible Buddha-fields.

And suppose one were to serve each individual Tathāgata, together with his bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, for as many eons as there are atoms in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of inexpressible Buddha-fields, providing them with robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick;

and suppose one were to offer to each individual Tathāgata every single day world-systems as numerous as the atoms in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of inexpressible Buddha-fields, filled with the *vaśirāja* jewel-kings.
Having performed [the preparations], one should give the gift.
Or, suppose another bodhisattva, being devoted to this Dharma-discourse, were to give even a single morsel of food to a sentient being, even one belonging to the animal realm;
compared to this accumulation of merit, the previous accumulation of merit consisting of the gifts of those bodhisattvas does not approach even a hundredth part.
Even a thousandth part,
even a hundred-thousandth part,
even a numerical fraction—
Not even a fraction, not even a calculation, not even a comparison.
It does not even tolerate the mention of the *upaniṣad*.
For what reason?
Because for irreversible bodhisattvas, this is the seal: namely, the hearing of this Dharma discourse.
Mañjuśrī, if one bodhisattva were to establish all sentient beings in all world-systems throughout the ten directions in the state of a follower by faith (śraddhānusārin),

and another bodhisattva were to establish a single sentient being in the state of a follower of the Dharma through meaning (arthānusārin), this latter bodhisattva generates incalculably more merit than the former.
Mañjuśrī, if one bodhisattva were to establish all sentient beings in all world-systems throughout the ten directions in the state of following after the meaning (*arthānusāritva*),
and another bodhisattva were to establish a single sentient being in the state of following after the Dharma (*dharmānusāritva*),
this latter one generates incalculably more merit than the former.
Mañjuśrī, if one bodhisattva were to establish all sentient beings in all world-systems throughout the ten directions in the state of following the Dharma,
and another bodhisattva were to establish a single sentient being in the fruit of stream-entry, this latter bodhisattva generates incalculably more merit than the former.
Mañjuśrī, if a bodhisattva were to establish all sentient beings in all world-systems in the ten directions in the fruit of stream-entry,
and another bodhisattva were to establish a single sentient being in the fruit of once-returning,
this latter one generates incalculably more merit than the former.
Mañjuśrī, if a bodhisattva were to establish all sentient beings in all world-systems in the ten directions in the fruit of a once-returner,
and another bodhisattva were to establish a single sentient being in the fruit of a non-returner,
this latter one generates incalculably more merit than the former.
Mañjuśrī, if a bodhisattva were to establish all sentient beings in all world-systems in the ten directions in the fruit of a non-returner,
and another bodhisattva were to establish a single sentient being in arhatship,
this latter one generates incalculably more merit than the former.
Mañjuśrī, if one bodhisattva were to establish all sentient beings in all world-systems throughout the ten directions in the state of an Arhat,
and another bodhisattva were to establish a single sentient being in the state of a Pratyekabuddha,
this latter one generates incalculably more merit than the former.
Mañjuśrī, if a bodhisattva were to establish all sentient beings in all world-systems in the ten directions in the state of a pratyekabuddha,
and another bodhisattva were to establish even a single sentient being in the thought of awakening (bodhicitta),
the latter would generate incalculably more merit than the former.
Mañjuśrī, if a bodhisattva were to establish all sentient beings in all world-systems in the ten directions in the thought of awakening,
and another bodhisattva were to establish even a single sentient being in the state of non-retrogression,
the latter would generate far more merit than the former.
Mañjuśrī, if a bodhisattva were to establish all sentient beings in the state of non-retrogression,

and another bodhisattva, having gained faith in this Dharma-discourse, were to have it written down and extensively proclaim it to others, even causing a single sentient being to enter into this Dharma-discourse; [the latter would generate greater merit].
This person would generate much more merit than that.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"If a bodhisattva were to uphold the true Dharma of ten billion Buddhas during the final age of destruction,
and another were to listen to this sutra with reverence, the merit of the latter would be far more distinguished than that of the former."

Suppose someone, having traversed the ten directions by means of their supernatural power, were to worship ten million Buddhas and cause all people to pay homage to them, out of compassion and without attachment to any pleasures.

And whoever, with a serene mind, should teach this sūtra indicating the qualities of the Victors to another for even a moment within the teaching of the Sugata— the fruit of merit from that is far superior.
Having revealed this sutra proclaimed by the Sugata, which serves as a lamp for gods and humans,
he— possessing sharp wisdom and great power— swiftly attains the stage of the Buddhas.
Having heard such a discourse of the Sugatas, whoever should cause it to be heard by a second being—
even when those Buddhas, the supreme among men, have passed away into the realm of Nirvana without remainder— [that person shall attain the same merit].
Erect stupas that are lofty and beautiful, adorned with exquisite jewels reaching as far as the peak of existence;
surrounded by parasols, banners, and the sounds of bells, let them extend in circumference all the way to the summit of existence.
Suppose some bodhisattva here, having heard such a sūtra as this, were to establish it either in their own body or in a book; the fruit of merit from that would be far more distinguished.
The bodhisattva who upholds this Dharma— free from the stain of envy and confident—
shall indeed possess immeasurable merit and shall attain awakening according to his wish.
For this sūtra is praised and embraced by the Sugatas and by many bodhisattvas;
indeed, the very embodiment of the Tathāgatas is displayed here within the entire realm of space.

The Blessed One spoke thus; and the noble Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas assembled from the infinite, boundless, and entire world-systems of the ten directions, as well as the great Śrāvakas and the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
The Mahāyāna sūtra entitled *Ārya-sarvabuddhaviṣayāvatārajñānālokālaṃkāra* is completed.
Of those phenomena that arise from causes, the Tathāgata has explained their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.

This is the religious gift of the monk Śīladhvaja, a follower of the most excellent Mahāyāna. May the merit therein, preceded by [the dedication for] his teachers, preceptors, mother, and father, lead to the attainment of the fruit of unsurpassed knowledge for the entire mass of sentient beings.
This was written on the [specified] day of the month of Śrāvaṇa in the year of the reign of the illustrious Gopāladeva, the Great King of Kings, by the attendant Cāṇḍoka. Śrī!
